```python
import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Value plus pool premium times the count of other items that greedily fit in the post-take residual, standardised."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    R = float(remaining)
    k = v.shape[0]
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    prem = max(float(np.median(v - w)), 0.0)
    order = np.argsort(w, kind='stable')
    w_sorted = w[order]
    P = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(w_sorted)))
    p = np.empty(k, dtype=float)
    p[order] = np.arange(k, dtype=float)
    B = R - w
    m1 = np.searchsorted(P, B, side='right') - 1
    m2 = np.searchsorted(P, B + w, side='right') - 2
    cnt = np.clip(np.maximum(np.minimum(m1, p), m2), 0, k - 1)
    score = v + prem * cnt
    sd = score.std()
    return (score - score.mean()) / (sd + 1e-9)
```

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Regret of taking each candidate: its value minus the fractional greedy density fill of the residual after taking it, z-scored across candidates."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    weights = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    k = values.shape[0]
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    d = values / np.maximum(weights, 1.0)
    order = np.argsort(-d, kind="stable")
    ds = d[order]
    ws = weights[order]
    vs = values[order]
    PW = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(ws)))
    PV = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(vs)))
    B = remaining - weights  # residual capacity after taking each candidate
    m = np.clip(np.searchsorted(PW, B, side="right") - 1, 0, k - 1)
    fill = PV[m] + ds[m] * (B - PW[m])
    regret = values - fill
    sd = regret.std() + 1e-9
    return (regret - regret.mean()) / sd
```

This computes, for each candidate, its value minus the fractional greedy density fill of the residual capacity after taking it (sorted by density descending, with a fractional last item), then z-scores those regrets across candidates; I read "R" as `remaining` and used a stable descending sort so ties keep index order.

```python
    d_sorted = d[order]
```

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Standardised count of near-substitute weights (Gaussian kernel, bandwidth 5% of mean weight) among the other candidates."""
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    k = w.shape[0]

    delta = max(1.0, 0.05 * w.mean())

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):

import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Value excess over the pool density, but excess only counts when the item's weight is small enough to leave the pool still explorable; scaled by the pool's density spread."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    R = float(remaining)
    if v.size == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    R = max(R, 1.0)
    # pool density (value per unit weight over the remaining candidates)
    pool_w = w.sum()
    pool_v = v.sum()
    density = pool_v / pool_w if pool_w > 0 else 0.0
    excess = v - density * w
    # local density spread of the pool: how heterogeneous the pool is
    dens = v / np.maximum(w, 1.0)
    spread = dens.std() / (abs(dens.mean()) + 1e-9)
    spread = min(spread, 1.0)
    # how much of the remaining capacity this item would consume
    fill = np.minimum(w / R, 1.0)
    # when the pool is homogeneous (spread small), overweight the excess;
    # when heterogeneous, penalise big fills so cheap-but-heavy items do not hog capacity
    gate = (1.0 - spread) - spread * fill
    return np.tanh(gate * excess / (np.abs(excess).max() + 1e-9))
feature.measures: Value excess over the pool density, but excess only counts when the item's weight is small enough to leave the pool still explorable; scaled by the pool's density spread.

import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Value-per-weight ratio, but measured against the density the remaining capacity still needs to reach the global best rate: how much this item overshoots or undershoots the rate implied by the slack left over."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    R = float(max(remaining, 1.0))
    C = float(capacity) if capacity else 1.0
    d = v / np.maximum(w, 1.0)
    # the best achievable rate in the pool: target density for filling the rest
    target = d.max()
    if target <= 0:
        return np.zeros_like(d)
    # implied rate if this item is taken: it consumes weight w at rate d; the
    # leftover R-w must then be filled at whatever rate remains. A candidate is
    # good when its own rate is high AND it does not force the residual to be
    # filled far above the achievable target (i.e. it doesn't hog scarce capacity).
    leftover = np.maximum(R - w, 0.0)
    # required rate on the leftover to still hit "target on the whole remainder"
    required = (target * R - v) / np.maximum(leftover, 1e-9)
    # closeness of the required residual rate to the target, signed
    gap = (target - required) / (abs(target) + 1e-9)
    # blend with the plain relative density so high-rate items still lead
    rel = d / (target + 1e-9)
    return np.tanh(rel - 0.5 * np.tanh(gap))

import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Regret of a candidate against the best-value alternative that fits afterwards, weighted by how tightly the pair fills the remaining capacity: pairs that pack the residual are discounted."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    k = v.size
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    rem = max(float(remaining), 1.0)
    cap = max(float(capacity), 1.0)
    vm = v.max() if k > 0 else 0.0
    if vm <= 0.0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    r = np.clip(rem - w, 0.0, None)              # residual after taking i
    F = (w[None, :] <= r[:, None])               # (k,k): j still fits after i
    F[np.arange(k), np.arange(k)] = False        # exclude i itself
    # how much of the residual a follow-up j would consume, in [0,1]
    fill = np.clip(w[None, :] / np.maximum(r[:, None], 1.0), 0.0, 1.0)
    # a follow-up that fills the residual well is a strong alternative: boost it
    boost = 1.0 + 0.5 * fill * fill
    alt = np.where(F, v[None, :] * boost, 0.0).max(axis=1)
    # tie-break by the candidate's own residual share of the total capacity:
    # slightly prefer candidates leaving a residual that is a "nice" fraction
    own_fill = np.clip(w / rem, 0.0, 1.0)
    return np.clip((v - alt) / vm, -1.0, 1.0) + 0.05 * own_fill
feature.measures: Regret of a candidate against the best-value alternative that fits afterwards, weighted by how tightly the pair fills the remaining capacity: pairs that pack the residual are discounted.

import numpy as np
import math

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Local density contrast: how much a candidate's density exceeds the best density among items it would crowd out by consuming weight."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    R = max(float(remaining), 1.0)
    k = v.size
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    dens = v / np.maximum(w, 1.0)
    # For each candidate, look at items that are "lighter and only fit once it's taken"
    # proxied by: the best density among strictly lighter items still in the pool.
    # If a candidate is heavy, taking it removes budget that lighter items (with
    # potentially higher density) could have used.
    order = np.argsort(w)
    sorted_dens = dens[order]
    sorted_w = w[order]
    # running max density among items strictly lighter than each candidate
    # prefix max over sorted-by-weight ordering
    pref_max = np.maximum.accumulate(sorted_dens)
    # best density among strictly lighter items = prefix max up to previous weight
    lighter_best = np.zeros(k)
    lighter_best[order[1:]] = pref_max[:-1]
    # weight penalty: how much of remaining capacity the item consumes
    consume = w / R
    # contrast: positive when candidate beats lighter alternatives, negative when
    # a lighter item with higher density would be crowded out
    contrast = dens - lighter_best
    scale = np.abs(contrast).max()
    scale = scale if scale > 0 else 1.0
    return np.tanh(contrast / scale) * (1.0 - consume)
feature.measures: Local density contrast: how much a candidate's density exceeds the best density among items it would crowd out by consuming weight.

## Certificates the engine can check (for features)

- `inert`: it gives every candidate the same value in every decision, so it can't change a choice;
- `duplicate` (with `of`: a feature id): it ranks candidates exactly like that feature (up to sign or a monotone transform);
- `span`: within every decision it is a linear combination of the kept features, so it can only re-weight them.

The engine has already tested these against every evaluated feature on sampled decisions. You see each feature's code, the kept features' code, and the nearest match the engine found. Look for what it might have missed: algebraic identities, a feature equal to another up to a monotone transform on the problem's actual inputs, a condition that is never true for the problem's inputs.

# The problem: 0/1 knapsack, built item by item

There are n items, each with a positive integer value and weight, and one knapsack with a weight capacity. A solution is a set of items whose total weight is at most the capacity; the goal is the largest total value. Each item is taken at most once.

The solution is built one item at a time. One **decision** = choosing the next item to add; the **candidates** are all items not yet taken whose weight still fits in the remaining capacity, in their original index order. The chosen item is added for good (nothing is ever removed) and the build stops when no remaining item fits.

Four training families (Pisinger's classic generators), 100-200 items each, weights in 1-1000, capacity = half the total weight: `uncorrelated` (value uniform in 1-1000, independent of weight), `weakly_correlated` (value within ±100 of the weight, at least 1), `strongly_correlated` (value = weight + 100), `inverse_strongly_correlated` (weight = value + 100). The **gap** of an instance is 1 − value ÷ the optimal value (exact, by dynamic programming), in %.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `values`: shape (k,), int: the value of every candidate item (the items not yet taken that still fit), in index order.
- `weights`: shape (k,), int: their weights (each ≤ `remaining`).
- `remaining`: int: the capacity still free.
- `capacity`: int: the knapsack's total capacity (it differs between instances: normalise by it).
- `taken`: int: how many items have been added so far.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)), roughly in [-1, 1].
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

import numpy as np
import math

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Local density contrast: how much a candidate's density exceeds the best density among items it would crowd out by consuming weight."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    R = max(float(remaining), 1.0)
    k = v.size
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    dens = v / np.maximum(w, 1.0)
    # For each candidate, look at items that are "lighter and only fit once it's taken"
    # proxied by: the best density among strictly lighter items still in the pool.
    # If a candidate is heavy, taking it removes budget that lighter items (with
    # potentially higher density) could have used.
    order = np.argsort(w)
    sorted_dens = dens[order]
    sorted_w = w[order]
    # running max density among items strictly lighter than each candidate
    # prefix max over sorted-by-weight ordering
    pref_max = np.maximum.accumulate(sorted_dens)
    # best density among strictly lighter items = prefix max up to previous weight
    lighter_best = np.zeros(k)
    lighter_best[order[1:]] = pref_max[:-1]
    # weight penalty: how much of remaining capacity the item consumes
    consume = w / R
    # contrast: positive when candidate beats lighter alternatives, negative when
    # a lighter item with higher density would be crowded out
    contrast = dens - lighter_best
    scale = np.abs(contrast).max()
    scale = scale if scale > 0 else 1.0
    return np.tanh(contrast / scale) * (1.0 - consume)
feature.measures: Local density contrast: how much a candidate's density exceeds the best density among items it would crowd out by consuming weight.

import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Regret of a candidate against the best-value alternative that fits afterwards, weighted by how tightly the pair fills the remaining capacity: pairs that pack the residual are discounted."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    k = v.size
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    rem = max(float(remaining), 1.0)
    cap = max(float(capacity), 1.0)
    vm = v.max() if k > 0 else 0.0
    if vm <= 0.0:
        return np.zeros(k)
    r = np.clip(rem - w, 0.0, None)              # residual after taking i
    F = (w[None, :] <= r[:, None])               # (k,k): j still fits after i
    F[np.arange(k), np.arange(k)] = False        # exclude i itself
    # how much of the residual a follow-up j would consume, in [0,1]
    fill = np.clip(w[None, :] / np.maximum(r[:, None], 1.0), 0.0, 1.0)
    # a follow-up that fills the residual well is a strong alternative: boost it
    boost = 1.0 + 0.5 * fill * fill
    alt = np.where(F, v[None, :] * boost, 0.0).max(axis=1)
    # tie-break by the candidate's own residual share of the total capacity:
    # slightly prefer candidates leaving a residual that is a "nice" fraction
    own_fill = np.clip(w / rem, 0.0, 1.0)
    return np.clip((v - alt) / vm, -1.0, 1.0) + 0.05 * own_fill
feature.measures: Regret of a candidate against the best-value alternative that fits afterwards, weighted by how tightly the pair fills the remaining capacity: pairs that pack the residual are discounted.

import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Value excess over the pool density, but excess only counts when the item's weight is small enough to leave the pool still explorable; scaled by the pool's density spread."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    R = float(remaining)
    if v.size == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    R = max(R, 1.0)
    # pool density (value per unit weight over the remaining candidates)
    pool_w = w.sum()
    pool_v = v.sum()
    density = pool_v / pool_w if pool_w > 0 else 0.0
    excess = v - density * w
    # local density spread of the pool: how heterogeneous the pool is
    dens = v / np.maximum(w, 1.0)
    spread = dens.std() / (abs(dens.mean()) + 1e-9)
    spread = min(spread, 1.0)
    # how much of the remaining capacity this item would consume
    fill = np.minimum(w / R, 1.0)
    # when the pool is homogeneous (spread small), overweight the excess;
    # when heterogeneous, penalise big fills so cheap-but-heavy items do not hog capacity
    gate = (1.0 - spread) - spread * fill
    return np.tanh(gate * excess / (np.abs(excess).max() + 1e-9))
feature.measures: Value excess over the pool density, but excess only counts when the item's weight is small enough to leave the pool still explorable; scaled by the pool's density spread.

import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Value-per-weight ratio, but measured against the density the remaining capacity still needs to reach the global best rate: how much this item overshoots or undershoots the rate implied by the slack left over."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    R = float(max(remaining, 1.0))
    C = float(capacity) if capacity else 1.0
    d = v / np.maximum(w, 1.0)
    # the best achievable rate in the pool: target density for filling the rest
    target = d.max()
    if target <= 0:
        return np.zeros_like(d)
    # implied rate if this item is taken: it consumes weight w at rate d; the
    # leftover R-w must then be filled at whatever rate remains. A candidate is
    # good when its own rate is high AND it does not force the residual to be
    # filled far above the achievable target (i.e. it doesn't hog scarce capacity).
    leftover = np.maximum(R - w, 0.0)
    # required rate on the leftover to still hit "target on the whole remainder"
    required = (target * R - v) / np.maximum(leftover, 1e-9)
    # closeness of the required residual rate to the target, signed
    gap = (target - required) / (abs(target) + 1e-9)
    # blend with the plain relative density so high-rate items still lead
    rel = d / (target + 1e-9)
    return np.tanh(rel - 0.5 * np.tanh(gap))

name: density_target_residual_consistency

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Value plus pool premium times the count of other items that greedily fit in the post-take residual, standardised."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)

import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Density excess of each candidate over the capacity-weighted mean density of the other items fitting the post-take residual, scaled by residual fill fraction."""
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    w = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    d = v / np.maximum(w, 1.0)

    order = np.argsort(w, kind='stable')
    w_sorted = w[order]
    d_sorted = d[order]

    SW = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(w_sorted)))
    SD = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum((d_sorted * w_sorted))))

    p = np.empty(w.shape[0], dtype=np.int64)
    p[order] = np.arange(w.shape[0])

    B = remaining - w
    m = np.searchsorted(w_sorted, B, side='right')

    incl = (p < m)
    Wf = SW[m] - incl * w
    Df = SD[m] - incl * d * w

    d_mean = d.mean() if d.size > 0 else 0.0
    Dfill = np.where(Wf > 0, Df / np.where(Wf > 0, Wf, 1.0), d_mean)

    std = d.std()
    excess = (d - Dfill) / (std + 1e-9)

    # residual fill fraction: how much of the post-take residual the fitting pool can cover
    cap = max(float(capacity), 1.0)
    fill = np.clip(Wf / np.maximum(B, 1.0), 0.0, 1.0)

    out = excess * fill
    return np.clip(out, -3.0, 3.0)

import numpy as np

def feature(values, weights, remaining, capacity, taken):
    """Regret of taking each candidate: its value minus the fractional greedy density fill of the residual after taking it, z-scored across candidates."""
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    weights = np.asarray(weights, dtype=float)
    k = values.shape[0]
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    d = values / np.maximum(weights, 1.0)
    order = np.argsort(-d, kind="stable")
    ds = d[order]
    ws = weights[order]
    vs = values[order]
    PW = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(ws)))
    PV = np.concatenate(([0.0], np.cumsum(vs)))
    B = remaining - weights  # residual capacity after taking each candidate
    m = np.clip(np.searchsorted(PW, B, side="right") - 1, 0, k - 1)
    fill = PV[m] + ds[m] * (B - PW[m])
    regret = values - fill
    sd = regret.std() + 1e-9
    return (regret - regret.mean()) / sd

nodes.description: Reward a candidate whose weight leaves a residual that some other remaining candidate can fill almost exactly, targeting the strong-correlation tie-breaking.

nodes.title: pool rank percentile
nodes.description: Rank candidates by their position in the pool's value and weight order statistics (scale-free percentile blend), not by any ratio.

nodes.title: value minus best-alternative
nodes.description: Score each candidate by its value minus the best value achievable by the items that would still fit after taking it, a regret-style lookahead under tight capacity.

nodes.title: residual exactness for flat densities
nodes.description: When densities are near-equal (strong correlation), rank by how exactly the candidate's weight plus some other candidate's weight fills the residual, breaking density ties toward exact packing.

nodes.title: scarcity of post-take pool
nodes.description: Score a candidate by the density of the best item that remains available after taking it, so items that do not starve the pool of good future picks are preferred.

nodes.title: premium-aware residual packing
nodes.description: Candidate value plus the pool's per-item premium (median of v minus w, clipped at 0) times the maximum number of items the post-take residual can still hold, as an estimate of total realised value.

nodes.title: weight crowding substitutes
nodes.description: Score candidates by how many remaining items have near-identical weight (crowdedness of their weight neighbourhood), preserving the pool's ability to complete a fill.

nodes.title: wide find: density_contrast_vs_lighter
nodes.description: Local density contrast: how much a candidate's density exceeds the best density among items it would crowd out by consuming weight.
